STRENGTHS: (1) Clear, well-evidenced pain point: 31 interviews, 26 reported same-week staffing gaps and 19 reported lost revenue or rush premiums. (2) Early real traction: one paying client, 37 shifts filled, $5,180 labor spend, $622 fees, 5.5-hour average fill time, and ~60 of 140 registered workers active. This is more than most student ventures show. (3) Founder-market fit and complementary team: the CEO has direct banquet and catering experience, the CTO built a working prototype, and the COO covers operations, vetting and payments. (4) Sensible wedge and positioning: narrow focus on event roles, same-day matching, instant worker pay, and importing the caterer's own roster to ease switching from informal networks. (5) Plausible unit economics on paper: 12% fee, ~$13 contribution per shift, low stated CAC, and a modest ask ($25K) tied to a concrete pilot with measurable goals (6+ repeat caterers, >90% fill rate). (6) Intellectual honesty: the plan openly flags small-sample market sizing, untested pricing, single-client validation, and worker classification risk.

WEAKNESSES: (1) Thin validation: all usage, retention and pricing evidence comes from one client over six weeks. Projections (12 caterers, 1,800 shifts/month, ~$30K monthly revenue) are extrapolations from n=1, and the $13/shift and 40-shifts-per-month assumptions are unproven (the first client averaged ~6 shifts/week, roughly 25-30/month at best). (2) Regulatory/legal risk is existential: worker classification (employee vs. contractor), payroll taxes, workers' comp and state-by-state rules could break the model or add major cost; this is unresolved and no compliance advisor is on board. (3) Weak defensibility: the main competitor is a free informal network, larger marketplaces could add event features, and multi-sided density in a single metro is hard to build and easy to disintermediate (caterers and workers can transact off-platform once matched). (4) Market sizing is rough and bottom-up from a small sample; the metro TAM (~$16.8M) is small, so the beachhead supports only a modest business, and national extrapolation is a simple population scaling. (5) Economics likely understated: fee collected on top of labor with instant worker payout creates float/working-capital and credit risk, background checks, payment minimums, support and fraud/no-show costs are not in contribution margin; the 12% fee is untested and the 2.5% processing figure may not include these. (6) Marketplace cold-start and supply reliability: ~43% of registered workers have completed a shift, and the 90% fill-rate target must hold as demand scales across weekends and peak seasons. (7) Resource constraints: ~$11K cash remaining, founders are students with limited runway and no outside advisors, sales are founder-led, and equal equity with no stated vesting or governance detail.

OVERALL ASSESSMENT: A credible, honestly framed early-stage venture with real customer pain, a relevant team, and early paid traction, but with unproven scalability, a serious unresolved labor-compliance risk, and modest defensibility. Interest is moderate-to-positive: attractive as a small, milestone-driven pilot investment where the next 3 months of repeat-usage, fill-rate and classification-review evidence would materially de-risk the thesis.

Business plan text:

Rosterforge
Rosterforge Executive Summary
Problem
Small and mid-sized caterers run on thin margins and tight timelines, and their largest
operational risk is a short-staffed event. In interviews with 31 caterers and event-staffing
managers in our university's metro area, 26 said they had experienced a same-week staffing gap
in the previous quarter, and 19 said they had lost revenue or paid rush premiums because of
one. A typical event needs between four and fifteen part-time workers, such as bartenders,
servers, and setup or breakdown crews. Cancellations of 10 to 15 percent are normal, and most
caterers fill the gaps through group text threads, calls to former employees, and referrals.
This is slow, depends on a few individuals, and leaves no record of who is reliable. Payment is
a second friction: workers are paid by cash or by payroll that arrives one to two weeks after
the shift, which makes the best workers less willing to take short-notice work.
Solution
Rosterforge is a mobile and web app that turns an unfilled shift into a filled one within
hours. A caterer posts a shift with role, start time, duration, location and hourly rate. The
app notifies matching workers who have set their availability and role preferences, ranks them
by proximity, past ratings and reliability, and confirms the first acceptance. On the day,
workers check in with a location-verified tap. When the caterer confirms hours at the end of
the shift, the worker is paid immediately through a payments partner, and the caterer is billed
the same amount plus our fee. Caterers can also build a private roster of favorite workers who
are offered shifts first, which gives them the convenience of their existing contacts with the
reach of a larger pool.
Market
We are starting with caterers serving weddings, corporate events and private parties in a
single metropolitan area. Using public industry counts and our interviews, we estimate roughly
420 catering businesses in our launch metro, of which about 250 employ part-time event staff.
If the average such caterer books 60 events per year and fills eight roles per event, the metro
represents about 120,000 shifts per year. At an average shift value of 140 dollars, that is
roughly 16.8 million dollars in annual labor spend in our beachhead market. Our national
estimate, scaling by population from the same assumptions, is a staffing spend in the low
billions of dollars. These figures are rough, built from a small interview sample, and we plan
to refine them during the pilot.
Business Model
We charge caterers a service fee of 12 percent of the shift's labor cost, collected on top of
worker pay, and workers pay nothing. Early pricing is based on conversations rather than tests,
and we expect to adjust it after the pilot. At an average shift value of 140 dollars, revenue
is about 16.80 dollars per shift before payment-processing costs of roughly 2.5 percent,
leaving a contribution margin near 13 dollars per shift. A caterer filling 40 shifts per month
through Rosterforge would generate about 520 dollars in monthly contribution. We assume an
acquisition cost of 400 dollars per caterer through direct outreach and referrals, which
implies a payback of under one month if usage reaches that level. We have not yet validated
that usage level beyond our first client. We may later add a premium tier with roster analytics
and compliance tools.
Competition
The space is crowded. General-purpose shift-scheduling tools serve restaurants and retail but
do not supply workers. On-demand staffing marketplaces supply workers across many industries
but tend to focus on warehousing and hospitality agencies with minimum contracts and higher
fees. Traditional staffing agencies charge markups of 30 to 50 percent and respond in days.

Finally, caterers' informal networks are free and familiar, and they are our most significant
competitor. Our differentiation is a narrow focus on event roles, a same-day matching workflow,
instant worker payment, and the ability to bring a caterer's own workers onto the platform. We
recognize that larger marketplaces could add similar features, and our defensibility will
depend on local density of workers and caterers and on switching costs created by caterers'
saved rosters and records.
Team
Maya Okonkwo-Reyes, chief executive officer, is a senior in business administration who worked
three summers as a banquet captain and catering coordinator, and has personally dealt with
last-minute staffing gaps. Daniel Brandvold, chief technology officer, is a senior in computer
science who built the prototype and previously interned as a mobile developer. Priya
Venkataraman, chief operating officer, is a master's student in operations management who leads
worker vetting, caterer onboarding and payments integration. We have no outside advisors yet
and are seeking one with experience in labor compliance.
Milestones and Financials
We completed 31 customer-discovery interviews, built a working prototype for mobile and web,
and incorporated as a Delaware C corporation with equal founder equity. We raised 18,000
dollars from friends and family in a pre-seed round, of which about 11,000 dollars remains. Our
first client, a caterer with a staff of about 20, has paid us for six weeks of use, filling 37
shifts for 5,180 dollars in labor spend and generating 622 dollars in fees. We have a pool of
about 140 registered workers, of whom roughly 60 have completed at least one shift. Fill time
on those 37 shifts averaged 5.5 hours. Over the next twelve months we project 12 active
caterers, 1,800 shifts per month by month twelve, and monthly revenue of about 30,000 dollars
by year end. These projections assume rates of signup and repeat use that we have only observed
with one client, and we regard them as targets rather than forecasts. Our largest costs are
founder-led sales, payments and background-check fees, and part-time development help.
What We Ask For
We are applying for the competition's prize funding and mentoring. A 25,000 dollar award would
let us run a structured three-month pilot with 8 to 10 additional caterers, pay for background
checks and payment-processing minimums, and engage legal counsel to review worker
classification rules, which we know vary by state and represent a real risk to our model.
Beyond funding, we would value introductions to caterers and venue managers, advice on labor
compliance, and feedback on our pricing. Our goal is to show, by the end of the pilot, repeat
usage by at least six caterers and a fill rate above 90 percent, which would put us in a
position to raise a seed round.
